title: Cassini takes first close‑up images of Titan on Oct. 26, 2004
content:
On October 26, 2004, NASA’s Cassini spacecraft captured the first close-up images of Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. This second flyby brought the spacecraft significantly closer to the moon than its initial pass on July 3, 2004, reaching a distance of 745 miles (1,200 kilometers) from Titan’s surface at its closest point. During this encounter, Cassini took hundreds of photographs, providing the highest-resolution views of the hazy moon available at the time.

The images revealed a large continent-sized region that scientists named Xanadu. This area featured bright spots hinting at a mountain range, along with a large basin and smooth plains. Although astronomers were already aware that Titan possessed an atmosphere, these detailed photos depicted a world with characteristics reminiscent of what scientists suspect a young Earth may have been like.

Data collected during this flyby, including instrument observations, enabled scientists to measure Titan’s atmospheric density and composition. This information was critical for planning the trajectory and descent of the Huygens probe, a European spacecraft that had hitched a ride to the Saturn system with Cassini. The Huygens lander subsequently touched down on Titan in January 2005 to examine the surface directly.

Over its 13-year mission at Saturn, which concluded in 2017, Cassini completed 127 close flybys of Titan. These repeated observations allowed for extensive study of the moon’s surface and atmosphere, building on the foundational data gathered during the historic October 2004 encounter.
summary: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft captured the first close‑up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan, flying 745 miles (1,200 km) from the surface. The images revealed a continent‑sized region called Xanadu, with bright features suggesting a mountain range, a large basin, and smooth plains.

title: Jimmy Webb Reflects on Wild Days and Writing Hits for Dolly, Glen, and Frank
content: From Wichita Lineman to MacArthur Park, he penned masterpieces. As the great hit-maker resurrects his lost songs, he recalls writing for giants – and the night Richard Harris stripped off and disappeared ‘Flat for 50 miles,” recalls Jimmy Webb, remembering the desolate stretch of Oklahoma that inspired his classic song, Wichita Lineman. “Nothing out there except endless railroad tracks and telephone poles. Then suddenly there’s a guy at the top of one of the poles. He’s got his phone, he’s talking to somebody and then … whoosh! He goes by. I never saw him again, but I never forgot him.” Webb immortalised the unknown telephone worker’s solitude (and imagined conversation with a distant lover) with a 1968 smash hit for Glen Campbell. “But you wouldn’t believe what some people thought it was about,” chuckles the songwriter, now a chatty, self-effacing 80-year-old, video-calling from his kitchen in Long Island. “One guy who wrote to me thought it was about a football lineman, and a woman thought the young man in the song gets electrocuted because ‘the Wichita lineman is still on the line’.”
summary: Jimmy Webb, 80, reminisces about writing hits for Dolly, Glen Campbell, and Frank on a video call from his Long Island kitchen. He recalls the Oklahoma inspiration behind Wichita Lineman, the lost songs he resurrects, and the odd interpretations of the song’s meaning.

title: Writer Explains Why That Thing You Do! Is Their Feelgood Movie
content:
In a new installment of a series where writers discuss their most rewatched comfort films, the 1990s music comedy That Thing You Do! is highlighted as a standout feelgood choice. Written by Tom Hanks, the film is set in the 1960s and centers on a band’s journey to success. The article notes that the movie resonates deeply with viewers, particularly through moments that capture the essence of creative achievement.

A specific scene where Steve Zahn’s character asks his bandmate, “How did we get here?” before a live television performance, is cited as a pivotal moment that has lingered in the author’s mind for three decades. This question represents both an aspiration and a personal reflection for the writer. Additionally, the band’s reaction to hearing their song on the radio for the first time is described as one of the most ebullient scenes in film history.

The piece describes this moment as evoking a recognizable euphoria associated with creative accomplishment. The author argues that this shared human experience of joy in creation is what ultimately defines That Thing You Do! as their preferred comfort movie.
summary: Writer Explains Why That Thing You Do! Is Their Feelgood Movie.

title: ‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle America
content: Nathan Fielder’s three-hour Elizabeth Holmes film has become a pop culture phenomenon but at a sold-out Times Square screening, no one was quite sure what to think In You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villain Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the year When I see a film a second time during its theatrical run, it’s typically to take someone else who hasn’t yet seen it, at least in part hoping to witness their reaction to a piece of art that excited or moved me in some way. Seeing Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’s You Can See Everything a second time in New York City on a Saturday night was that impulse writ larger. This is a movie garnering a surprisingly sizable audience, and outsized audience reactions to go along with it; rewatching it in a full 300-seat auditorium offered the opportunity to re-experience that sense of discovery. Perhaps more to the point, almost everyone I knew had seen it already; all I could do was observe strangers. This documentary, peering into (and helping to create) a hall of mirrors around the famed med-tech scammer Elizabeth Holmes, has become the box office story of the fall, actually rising 25% on its second weekend to gross another $19.5m – a rare feat even given its expanded screen count. With over $45m in North America, it’s already one of A24’s biggest movies ever; it could wind up in the company’s top three, and way up on the list of the highest-grossing nonfiction features. If You Can See Everything isn’t quite an Obsession -level cash cow, it’s probably even more surprising that a three-hour documentary whose existence was only announced about eight weeks ago is on track to make more money than high-profile new releases like Practical Magic 2, Verity and Street Fighter, among others. It’s also outgrossed co-director Oppenheim’s fellow A24 surprise hit Primetime, which has the benefit of genuine movie star Robert Pattinson.
summary: ‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle America.

title: Mac DeMarco dazzles Carnegie Hall with glowing melodies and shirtless antics
content:
Mac DeMarco returned to New York’s Carnegie Hall on Sunday night for the first of two sold‑out shows, bringing his cult indie‑pop sound to the historic venue. The concert was marked by an energetic crowd of Gen Z fans, many accompanied by parental chaperones, and a group of bright‑eyed teens who had traveled from Wisconsin. Attendees were seen searching online for “Where to find Mac DeMarco after the concert” and joking about whether they might kiss The 1975’s frontman Matty Healy if given the chance.

The performance featured introspective anthems and a cover of a Michael Jackson song, underscoring DeMarco’s ability to blend familiar pop with his signature indie style. The show echoed the youthful excitement that first graced Carnegie Hall more than 68 years ago when Leonard Bernstein presented his first Young People’s Concert.

DeMarco’s early career, emerging from Vancouver in the early 2010s, was described as “party‑hardy” and “modern‑day Pigpen”‑like, with live sets that included Limp Bizkit covers and spontaneous audience make‑out sessions. The 2014 docu‑short Pepperoni Playboy captured this era, showing the artist and his band drinking champagne out of lobster shells and cliff‑diving amid a relentless touring schedule.
summary: Mac DeMarco delivered introspective anthems and a Michael Jackson cover at Carnegie Hall in New York. The first of two sold‑out performances drew a youthful crowd and was noted for its energetic atmosphere.

title: John Oliver Exposes Rise of Nazi References in Republican Party
content: Last Week Tonight host looked into the rise of bigotry and neo-nazism within the party before critical midterm races With just a week to go until the US midterm elections, John Oliver used the entirety of his latest Last Week Tonight episode to focus on a “worrying trend that’s been on the rise” within the Republican party, which has “found itself answering some uncomfortable questions about Nazi references”, from a New York congressional candidate posting a photo of his grandfather in his Nazi uniform to mega-donor Elon Musk’s infamous apparent Nazi salute at a Trump rally in 2025. “Everything about that screams, ‘Nazi!’” Oliver said of Musk’s gesture. “Well, almost everything. To be fair to the Nazis, unlike Elon, they at least looked sharp in their suits.”
summary: John Oliver used his latest Last Week Tonight episode to highlight a worrying trend of bigotry and neo‑nazism in the Republican party. He cited a New York congressional candidate posting a photo of his grandfather in a Nazi uniform and Elon Musk's apparent Nazi salute at a Trump rally in 2025.

title: England U-15s abandon World Cup match against Ireland over racism allegation
content:
England’s Under-15 squad abandoned their World Cup match against the Republic of Ireland on Monday in Baku, Azerbaijan, after a player alleged he was subjected to a racist slur. The Group C fixture was abandoned in the final minute with Ireland leading 4-1. Fifa has confirmed it is investigating the incident.

Footage captured an England player approaching the bench following an altercation. The player is believed to have claimed an opponent called him a “monkey” and raised a complaint with coaching staff. This prompted England head coach Matt Thorpe to approach the referee, leading to the team walking off the pitch rather than resuming the match.
summary: England players abandoned their Under-15 World Cup match against the Republic of Ireland after a player reported being subjected to a racist slur. Fifa confirmed it is investigating the incident, which occurred in the final minute of the Group C fixture in Baku, Azerbaijan.

title: Liam Dawson says England are gutted after ODI series setbacks
content:
Liam Dawson stated that England are “gutted” following two consecutive ODI defeats against Sri Lanka and Pakistan, which have put their chances of reaching the tri-series final in serious doubt. The spinner expressed the team’s desperation to win, noting that the dressing room is deeply disappointed by the recent setbacks.

Despite the losses, Dawson remains optimistic that these experiences will serve as useful learning opportunities for the squad ahead of the World Cup in southern Africa in 12 months’ time. To advance to the final, England must first see Pakistan defeat Sri Lanka on Tuesday before they can secure a significant victory over Sri Lanka themselves on Thursday.
summary: Liam Dawson revealed that England are desperate to win following agonising defeats to Sri Lanka and Pakistan. He stated that the team is optimistic these losses will serve as useful learning experiences ahead of the World Cup in 12 months.

title: 150+ ATP doubles players sign open letter to protect format from draw cuts
content: Plans to slash games by half and prize money criticised ‘Hard for players to build and sustain a doubles career’ More than 150 doubles players on the men’s ATP tour have signed an open letter addressed to the ATP board and management imploring the men’s tennis governing bodies to reconsider controversial doubles reforms and “protect” the format in professional tennis. The subject of potential reforms to the ATP has been a significant issue since players were informed in a meeting during Wimbledon that the ATP was conducting a review of its doubles regulations and potential changes could see doubles draws being halved at the ATP events in 2028. Under these proposals, ATP Masters 1000 events would host only 16 doubles teams and the main draws at ATP 500 and 250 events would accommodate only eight teams.
summary: 150+ ATP doubles players sign open letter to protect format from draw cuts.

title: Nate Silver: Polling Must Be Wrong for Republicans to Keep House Control
content: Pollster Nate Silver stated Sunday that polling “would have to be very wrong” for Republicans to maintain control of the House. Speaking a little over a week before this year’s midterms, Silver cited high turnout in Democratic primaries and early voting data as factors supporting his assessment.
summary: Pollster Nate Silver said that polling would have to be very wrong for Republicans to hold onto the House. He cited high turnout in Democratic primaries and early voting data as evidence.
author: The Hill

title: Republicans face costly competitive races despite gerrymandered district lines
content: Republicans redrew congressional district lines aiming to advantage their candidates in the upcoming midterms. Despite these efforts, the party now confronts costly and competitive races that they initially expected to avoid through strategic map changes.
summary: Republicans redrew congressional district lines to tilt the midterms in their favor. They are now facing expensive and competitive races they had hoped to outmaneuver.
author: NPR Politics

title: Redistricting isn't playing out how the GOP hoped. And, Brazil's Lula wins 4th term
content: Republicans are investing millions in the upcoming midterms, yet they may fail to capture districts that were drawn to favor their party. Meanwhile, Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a fourth term in office, marking a significant political comeback.
summary: Republicans are spending millions on the midterms but may not win districts drawn to favor them. Brazil's Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term in a stunning political comeback.
author: NPR Politics

title: Judge rules DOJ illegally fired Maurene Comey
content: A judge ruled that the Department of Justice illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey. Comey had worked as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan for about a decade. The ruling, which declares her dismissal unlawful, heightens concerns about politically motivated firings within the DOJ.
summary: Maurene Comey served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan for around a decade. A judicial ruling found her dismissal unlawful, raising concerns about politically motivated firings at the DOJ.
author: NPR Politics

title: Lula Re‑elected in Brazil, Boosting Hope for Zero Deforestation by 2030
content:
The re-election of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday has renewed optimism regarding the nation’s ability to meet its target of ending deforestation in all biomes by 2030. In a tight race against right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula secured an unprecedented fourth term in office. During his acceptance speech, the 81-year-old leader stated that Brazil would demonstrate how climate policy is handled in the country, noting that deforestation rates decreased annually during his previous four years in power.

Recent data from Brazil’s space agency indicates that forest-clearing in the Amazon reached its lowest level on record following the introduction of a deforestation action plan. This plan, introduced in 2023, constrained illegal cattle ranching from expanding into the rainforest. Carlos Nobre, a veteran Brazilian climate scientist and co-chair of the Science Panel for the Amazon, described the current situation as a “historic opportunity” to prevent the Amazon from reaching a tipping point where large sections could turn into savanna. He emphasized that while recent reductions in deforestation have been crucial, ending deforestation by 2030 and accelerating large-scale forest restoration remain urgent priorities.

Lula’s victory is also expected to bolster international fundraising efforts for rainforest protection. Brazil spearheaded the creation of the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF), a fund designed to raise public seed capital for investment in financial markets, with returns paid to rainforest countries. Despite being a developing nation, Brazil has pledged $1 billion to the fund and aims to help reach a $10 billion goal from governments by the end of the year. Anders Haug Larsen, advocacy director at the Norway Rainforest Foundation, described the election result as a “relief” that makes it more attractive for donors to support rainforest protection.

On Monday, the day following the election, the Netherlands announced a €500-million contribution to the TFFF, subject to parliamentary approval and to be disbursed over ten years. This pledge brings the total committed to the fund to $7.8 billion. Norway’s climate minister, Sigrun Aasland, expressed hope that the $10 billion milestone could be achieved by year’s end. Brazilian officials, who have led fundraising efforts, reported ongoing conversations with potential donors including China, Korea, and Japan.

Despite the positive outlook for environmental policy, political challenges remain. Veteran diplomat Bráulio Ferreira de Souza Dias noted that right-wing pro-Bolsonaro lawmakers have gained more seats in both legislative chambers, creating a difficult political scenario. Observatório do Clima, a network of Brazilian green groups, stated that seven out of ten representatives and senators in the next legislature are likely to vote against the climate and environmental agenda. Sonia Guajajara, former minister of Indigenous Peoples, highlighted the need to consolidate the 20 indigenous territories created under the current administration, deeming them essential for tackling the climate crisis.
summary: Lula Re‑elected in Brazil, Boosting Hope for Zero Deforestation by 2030.
author: Climate Home News

title: Jewish farmers in North Carolina continue 'Jewishly inspired' agrarian tradition
content:
In the United States, an increasing number of Jewish people are turning to farming for purpose and community. Wendy Rhein exemplifies this trend at her Chutzpah Hollow farm in Tryon, North Carolina, where she rounds up sheep among hazelnut and walnut trees.

Rhein’s routine includes calling her flock, “Hi, Brea. Come on down. I hear you,” as she manages a Barbados black belly ewe. When the ewe moves, the rest of the flock follows, illustrating the practical and communal aspects of her agrarian practice.
summary: Wendy Rhein, a Jewish farmer in Tryon, North Carolina, raises sheep among hazelnut and walnut trees at Chutzpah Hollow farm. Her practice reflects a growing trend of Jewish people seeking purpose and community through farming in the United States.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Typhoon Champi Declared Strongest Storm of Year So Far
content:
Typhoon Champi was declared the strongest storm of the year so far after recording sustained winds of 185 mph last week. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. The storm brought gusts of up to 141 mph and 48‑hour rainfall totals of more than 620 mm to parts of Yilan.

So far, the death toll remains at one, with 527 reported injured. Widespread power outages affected more than 288,000 houses at one point, although most had since been reconnected. The storm has been downgraded to a tropical storm as it rapidly weakens to the south‑west of Japan’s mainland on Monday.
summary: One dead and 527 injured as winds of up to 185mph hit Taiwan and southern Japan, while Greece issues flood alerts Typhoon Champi was declared the strongest storm of the year so far after recording sustained winds of 185mph last week. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Northwestern Medicine study finds unknown immune cells drive harmful eye vessel growth
content:
A Northwestern Medicine study has identified a previously unrecognized population of immune cells that appears to fuel harmful blood‑vessel growth in several blinding eye diseases. The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation.

The study’s senior author, Jeremy Lavine, M.D., Ph.D., an assistant professor of ophthalmology, said the discovery could open the door to new treatments for patients who do not respond to existing therapies.
summary: Northwestern Medicine study finds unknown immune cells drive harmful eye vessel growth.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Fructose slows liver tumors in mice when key sugar-processing gene is missing, may lead to new treatments
content:
A new study led by researchers at City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) has identified a previously unknown anticancer mechanism involving fructose. The research demonstrates that in the specific metabolic context of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), dietary fructose does not fuel tumor growth; instead, it suppresses it. This finding highlights a distinct metabolic role for fructose, which, despite its chemical similarity to glucose, is metabolized differently in the body.

The study underscores recent advances in understanding fructose metabolism and its regulatory functions in human health. By revealing how fructose can inhibit liver tumors in mice when a key sugar-processing gene is missing, the work positions fructose metabolism as a frontier topic in life sciences and medicine, potentially opening avenues for new treatments.
summary: Fructose is an important nutrient that, despite having a chemical structure very similar to that of glucose, is metabolized very differently in the body. Research into fructose metabolism and its regulation of metabolism in the human body has in recent years become a frontier topic in the life sciences and medicine.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Rat experiments show observing danger shapes learning
content: Rat experiments suggest that watching others face danger can shape learning. The article notes that much of what we know comes from experiences we have never had, that a child observes a parent’s reaction and it influences future actions, and that seeing another person in danger can make someone more cautious.
summary: Rat experiments suggest that observing others in danger can shape learning. The study shows that seeing another person in danger can make someone more cautious.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study Finds Single Violin Lesson Alters Brain Wave Patterns
content: A recent study employing wearable brain‑imaging technology examined how the human brain responds when a person learns to play a musical instrument. The researchers focused on violin players and discovered distinct patterns of brain activity that support instrument performance. Remarkably, just one lesson produced significant changes in those activity patterns.
summary: A study using wearable brain imaging showed how learning to play an instrument changes brain activity. The results revealed that a single violin lesson significantly alters patterns of brain activity.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Dark days cause fatigue, irritability, carb cravings in Britons
content: When daylight saving time ends in October, Britons receive an extra hour of sleep as the clocks go back. However, the earlier arrival of darkness in the evenings means that many people find this additional rest difficult to enjoy, as night falls before most have finished work.
summary: When clocks go back in October, millions of Britons welcome an extra hour in bed. But by evening, darkness arrives before many finish work, making that extra hour feel distant.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Tadalafil, Viagra's Cousin, May Help Muscle Cells Stay Primed for Regeneration
content:
Tadalafil: Uses and Athlete Adoption

Tadalafil is a prescription medication closely related to Viagra. It treats erectile dysfunction (ED) and the urinary symptoms associated with an enlarged prostate.  

Both competitive and recreational athletes sometimes use tadalafil to manage pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a condition that can limit the body’s exercise tolerance.
summary: Tadalafil is a prescription drug closely related to Viagra. It treats erectile dysfunction, urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate, and pulmonary arterial hypertension in athletes.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Rare Cancer Location Affects Survival, Study Finds
content: New research suggests that the location of a rare, aggressive cancer influences survival rates. The tumor, which commonly appears in the uterus, limbs, and abdomen, behaves differently depending on its site within the body. These findings highlight the importance of site‑specific treatment strategies.
summary: A new study shows that a rare, aggressive cancer behaves differently depending on its location in the body. The cancer is commonly found in the uterus, limbs, and abdomen, and its location may impact survival.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Article examines whether tipping on takeout orders is appropriate
content:
Adding a tip to a take‑out order is not always logical, yet the practice has become a social expectation. When you pick up a pizza, the credit‑card terminal often prompts you to tip and offers several options.  

The article notes that tipping a cashier who merely hands over the pizza feels odd, because the cashier’s role in the transaction is minimal. At the same time, refusing to tip can appear harsh or disrespectful, especially when the system encourages generosity.  

The piece asks readers to consider the right course of action, weighing the customary expectation against the practical reality of the cashier’s effort.
summary: The piece explains that adding a gratuity on takeout does not always make sense but has become a societal norm. It describes a typical pizza‑takeout scenario where a credit‑card screen prompts a tip, leaving customers to choose between tipping the cashier or selecting no tip.
author: Guardian Business

title: European gas prices hit four-year high of €97/MWh amid winter supply fears
content: European gas prices surged to a four‑year high, reaching €97 (£81) per megawatt‑hour on Monday. The rise is attributed to growing concerns over Middle East supply disruptions, spurred by reports that the United States and Israel are planning a strike on Iran. Traders have priced in stronger heating demand as temperatures across Europe fell, further lifting wholesale gas costs. The spike marks the highest level seen since 2022, reflecting heightened uncertainty about the continent’s winter supply.
summary: Wholesale European gas prices rose to €97 (£81) per megawatt‑hour on Monday, the highest level since 2022. The surge was driven by fears of further Middle East supply disruptions, including reports of US‑Israeli plans to strike Iran, and falling temperatures that increased heating demand.
author: Guardian Business

title: Anthropic files for IPO as Meta launches $95bn share sale to fund AI expansion
content: Meta says share sale will support its “continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”, as Elon Musk warns some AI cloud computing firms face ‘guppy-level death’ UK government borrowing costs are dropping this morning, a welcome sign ahead of Wednesday’s budget. The yield (or interest rate) on 10 and 30-year UK gilts have both dropped by around three basis points (0.03 of a percentage point) this morning. Issuing loans to public financial institutions creates a financial asset that offsets the increase in outstanding government debt. If the investments that the PuFins make generate sufficient returns for the PuFins to repay their government loans, then long term debt sustainability is little affected. Limited transparency and the risk that the PuFins may suffer impairments on their investments will probably make bond market investors skeptical of the extra gilt issuance. Chancellor Healey should avoid a big increase in gilt issuance to fund such intra-public sector lending. Nebius, CoreWeave and Iren were slammed in premarket trading on Monday after SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said more than 200 neoclouds are “going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.” That’s the guppy fish – prone to suddenly dying in household fisk tanks – not the GBPJPY FX cross... In a post on X Musk said “debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers”.

title: Data review of US economy under Trump’s second term as midterms near
content: As the U.S. midterm elections near, a new analysis uses five charts to examine the economic conditions of President Donald Trump’s second term. The piece notes that many Americans are focused on the economy, with voters described as “exhausted by years of higher prices.” It also recalls that Trump won the 2024 presidential election on pledges to lower inflation and to reverse what he characterized as economic damage caused by the preceding administration. The charts are presented as a data‑driven view of the current economic reality.
summary: As the US midterm elections approach, data is examined to assess the economy during Donald Trump's second term. Trump won the presidency in 2024 promising to lower inflation and reverse what he said was damage from the Biden administration.
author: Guardian Business

title: AI-powered robotic lab automates tasks for next‑generation heat‑resistant coating research
content: Researchers have created a self‑driving laboratory that merges artificial intelligence with robotics to automate tasks such as precise measurement and mixing of chemical ingredients, high‑temperature furnace processing, and sample retrieval. The system is intended to accelerate the discovery of next‑generation heat‑resistant coatings.
summary: Researchers have developed a self‑driving laboratory that combines artificial intelligence and robotics. The system automates laboratory tasks, including accurate measurement and mixing of chemical ingredients, high‑temperature furnace processing, and sample retrieval.

title: Millions of Americans keep memories of dead ancestors after Halloween
content:
Halloween signals the start of a series of religious and cultural festivals that honor the dead, including All Saints' Day, All Souls' Day, and the Day of the Dead.  

Even after the ghost and skeleton decorations are removed, deceased loved ones remain present in people’s social worlds.
summary: Halloween begins a series of religious and cultural festivals that honor the dead, such as All Saints' Day, All Souls' Day and the Day of the Dead. The article notes that deceased loved ones continue to exist in people's social worlds even after ghost and skeleton decorations are taken down.

title: Basel researchers find three chromosomal domain types in roundworm DNA
content: Researchers at the University of Basel have identified three distinct types of large chromosomal domains that organize DNA within cell nuclei. The finding, highlighted in a study of roundworms, adds to the understanding that nearly every cell contains roughly two meters (6.6 feet) of DNA that must remain both organized and accessible.
summary: Researchers at the University of Basel discovered three distinct types of large chromosomal domains that help organize DNA in nuclei. The discovery reveals greater complexity in how roundworms organize their DNA.

title: Scientists' research becomes less disruptive with age, yet lasting breakthroughs increase
content: A recent study reports that scientists tend to produce less disruptive research as they age, yet their breakthroughs are more likely to endure. The study notes that scientific progress usually occurs in incremental steps, with researchers building on prior discoveries. Occasionally, a breakthrough emerges that challenges conventional thinking and redirects a field.
summary: Scientists produce less disruptive research as they age, but their breakthroughs are more likely to last. Science often advances in small steps, with occasional breakthroughs that challenge conventional thinking and change the direction of a field.

title: Human composting explained: what it is and how it works
content: The article poses the question of what should happen to a body after death, noting it is a decision that will eventually have to be made by the individual or their loved ones. It introduces the concept of human composting, exploring how this method works.
summary: The article introduces human composting as a method for handling a body after death. It notes that deciding what to do with a body is a personal decision that may need to be made by the individual or their loved ones.

title: Botanists find new plant species each year in Gabon's rainforests, says Archange Boupoya
content:
Gabon's lush rainforests continue to produce new plant species each year, attracting botanists such as Archange Boupoya.  
Boupoya believes that cataloging this exceptional yet largely mysterious natural wealth is essential for its preservation.
summary: Each year Gabon's lush rainforests yield the discovery of previously unknown plant species to botanists such as Archange Boupoya. Boupoya says the exceptional yet largely mysterious natural wealth needs to be cataloged to be saved.

content: Recent research shows that cells transferred between mother and fetus during pregnancy can persist in the brain. Columnist Helen Thomson examines whether these microchimeric cells might affect development, health or behaviour, exploring the implications of this cellular legacy.

title: Satellites Provide Strong Evidence AMOC Has Slowed 14% Over 30 Years
content: Satellite observations provide strong evidence that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is weakening. An analysis of ocean heat release to the atmosphere indicates the system that transports warmth to Europe has slowed by 14 percent over the past 30 years.
summary: Satellite observations indicate that the Atlantic current system that warms Europe has slowed 14 percent over the past 30 years. The analysis of ocean heat release to the atmosphere provides strong evidence that the AMOC is weakening.

title: Adult brains can generate new neurons late in life, prompting health rethink
content: A controversial discovery that the human brain can generate new neurons surprisingly late in life is prompting a rethink of adult brain health. The finding points toward improved treatments for stroke, dementia, and depression.
summary: Scientists have controversially discovered that brains can generate new neurons surprisingly late in life. The finding is prompting a rethink of adult brain health and could lead to better treatments for stroke, dementia and depression.

title: Marine amphibian Gerrothorax maritimus discovered in Late Triassic China
content:
A fossil of Gerrothorax maritimus, a 74‑centimetre‑long marine amphibian, was uncovered in a national geopark in Guanling county, China.  The specimen, found by farmers, is almost perfectly preserved and represents the first evidence that an amphibian once adapted to fully oceanic life.  The discovery was reported by Ryosuke Motani of the University of California, Davis, and published in Nature Ecology & Evolution (DOI 10.1038/s41559-026-03209-9).

The researchers used strontium isotope ratios to confirm that the bones of G. maritimus carried a clear signature of seawater.  This indicates the animal grew to adulthood in the ocean rather than being a land‑dwelling organism washed in after death.  Palaeogeographic reconstructions place the site at least 30 kilometres from the nearest shoreline 237 million years ago, during the Late Triassic Period.  The fossil was recovered together with a 7‑metre ichthyosaur, Guizhouichthyosaurus, underscoring the marine context of the find.

Anatomically, G. maritimus was a flat, bottom‑dwelling ambush predator.  It possessed four legs and gills, features that distinguish it from fish and reptiles.  Its wide mouth and a robust hyoid bone in the neck suggest it used suction feeding, a strategy seen in modern bottom‑dwelling predators such as wobbegong sharks.  No evidence was found that the creature underwent metamorphosis, a common process in many modern amphibians.

The closest relative of G. maritimus, Gerrothorax pulcherrimus, lived in freshwater environments and was described nearly a century ago.  Motani argues that the marine lifestyle of G. maritimus was an accidental evolutionary outcome: the body armour that protected its freshwater ancestors also served as an impermeable barrier against saltwater.  He notes that “amphibious” does not necessarily mean the ability to live on land, citing modern newts that remain entirely aquatic.  John Long of Flinders University comments that, had reptiles not invaded the marine niche at the same time, amphibians might have diversified in the sea, but this did not occur.
summary: A 74‑centimetre fossil of the marine amphibian Gerrothorax maritimus was found by farmers in Guanling County, China, and identified as a bottom‑dwelling ambush predator from the Late Triassic seas. Isotope analysis showed the animal grew to adulthood in seawater, suggesting its strong body armour allowed it to survive in the ocean 237 million years ago.
author: New Scientist

title: Wind turbines kill nearly 19 million bats in US over 40 years
content: Hoary bats have been the worst affected of the 10 species the researchers studied Michael Durham/Nature Picture Library/Alamy Wind turbines have killed nearly 19 million bats in the US over the past four decades, according to the most comprehensive analysis of its kind to date. The problem seems to have worsened in recent years, with more than 1.5 million deaths now occurring annually. But there may be ways of making this green energy source safer for wildlife without overly affecting energy production. This data can help “advance research to really support effective conservation measures and science-driven decision-making in the future”, says Charles Labuzzetta at Fort Collins Science Center in Colorado. Endearing photos of bats show clever adaptations like long tongues Bats play a vital role in ecosystems, particularly by controlling insects like mosquitoes and moths that produce crop-killing caterpillars. But many species face growing threats from habitat loss, disease and human activities, with some now classified as threatened or endangered. Advertisement Wind turbines are one of these human-activity threats. Researchers have previously found large numbers of dead bats at wind farms during monitoring that is required to comply with wildlife protection regulations. But not all wind farms share their results, and monitoring methods vary from site to site, says team member Bethany Straw, also at Fort Collins Science Center. “We know bats are being impacted, but could we change the engineering or sites of a turbine to minimise those impacts?” she asks. “There’s been an increasing interest in this, but we just haven’t had the appropriate data yet.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter Now, Straw, Labuzzetta and their colleagues have analysed 499 reports from wind farms across the 48 adjoining US states to estimate how many bats were killed by turbines from 1981 to 2024, focusing on 10 species. They used a statistical model that considered differences in how wind farms searched for dead bats, the size and design of their turbines, and the surrounding environment. Their results suggest that wind turbines killed an estimated 18.7 million bats between 1981 and 2024. Annual deaths seem to have exceeded 1.5 million from 2021 onwards, which may be the result of more wind turbines being installed. Hoary bats ( Lasiurus cinereus ) had the greatest losses, with an estimated 6.7 million deaths, followed by 5.8 million deaths among eastern red bats ( Lasiurus borealis ), 3.4 million among silver-haired bats ( Lasionycteris noctivagans ) and 1.5 million among big brown bats ( Eptesicus fuscus ). Wind farms near rivers and turbines with longer blades were linked to more deaths among certain species, while having more space between the blades and the ground may reduce the risk. Don’t forget birds and bats when renovating or building new homes As newer homes are built or older homes are renovated, empty attic spaces are disappearing – this eliminates a vital refuge for birds and bats during a biodiversity crisis The researchers aren’t sure why bats fly so close to wind turbines. Previous work suggests that migratory bats mistake the structures for trees, and approach them in search of food, shelter or mates. A recent European study also found that male bats sometimes sing courtship songs around turbines, potentially attracting females into the path of spinning blades. Differences in species prevalence and behaviours may partly explain why some seem to be more at risk than others. The researchers hope their findings will help wind farm developers protect bats by choosing safer locations and adjusting turbine designs. Research suggests that stripy wind turbines could prevent seabird collisions, for instance. Changing when turbines operate might also help. Research shows that temporarily shutting them down during periods of high bat activity, particularly in low winds, can substantially reduce fatalities with limited loss of electricity production. Journal Reference: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2612674123
summary: Wind turbines kill nearly 19 million bats in US over 40 years.
author: New Scientist

title: MIT develops implantable ultrasound device to boost brain drug delivery for glioblastoma
content:
MIT researchers have introduced a new implantable device intended to improve drug delivery to the brain, particularly for patients with glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor. The device, named LUCID (Long‑term Ultrasound‑enhanced Convective Injection Device), combines a drug‑reservoir with an array of 24 miniature ultrasound transducers that generate sound waves at the tip of a 3‑D‑printed cannula. The ultrasound is designed to help drug molecules travel farther through brain tissue and to temporarily increase the permeability of the blood‑brain barrier.

The implant can be placed in the skull during tumor‑removal surgery. Its reservoir holds roughly 100 microliters of fluid, and drug infusion is driven by a passive osmotic pump. Ultrasound dosing is programmed wirelessly via a Bluetooth‑enabled controller, while a small rechargeable battery powers the transducers. According to senior author Canan Dagdeviren, an associate professor of media arts and sciences at MIT, the system offers clinicians flexibility in the size, length, and number of infusions.

In laboratory tests, the researchers demonstrated that ultrasound‑assisted delivery spread molecules significantly farther than passive diffusion alone. Experiments using a gel‑like “tissue phantom” and a mouse model—where an MRI contrast agent was delivered—showed enhanced distribution when the ultrasound array was activated. Lead author Sarah Ornellas noted that this localized, programmable enhancement could reduce systemic toxicity while improving drug reach within the target area.

Beyond small‑molecule chemotherapy, the team suggests the platform could deliver immunotherapies, nucleic acids, or gene‑therapy agents, and may be adaptable for soft‑tissue treatments in organs other than the brain. The study, published in the journal Device, lists co‑authors from MIT, Harvard Medical School, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston University and other institutions. Funding for the work came from the MIT Media Lab Consortium and the National Institutes of Health.
summary: MIT researchers designed an implantable drug‑delivery device that includes a reservoir and 24 ultrasound transducers to release drugs and enhance their spread in the brain. In tissue‑phantom tests and a mouse study, ultrasound activation increased molecule distribution, and the device can be programmed wirelessly via Bluetooth.
author: MIT News

title: Arctic winter sea ice could vanish faster, up to 1 million km² less than predicted
content: New research indicates Arctic winter sea ice may vanish faster than earlier expectations. The study used climate clues from 6,000‑year‑old ocean sediments compared with modern climate models, finding future winter ice coverage could be about one million square kilometers less than prior forecasts.
summary: New research using climate clues from 6,000 years ago indicates Arctic winter sea ice could disappear much faster than previously expected. Comparing ancient ocean sediments with modern climate models, researchers estimate future winter ice coverage may be about one million square kilometers smaller than earlier predictions.
author: Science Daily

title: AI system REDMOD spots pancreatic cancer signs 475 days before diagnosis
content: A new artificial‑intelligence system named REDMOD can detect pancreatic cancer long before it appears on standard imaging. The technology identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days prior to a formal diagnosis and demonstrated nearly double the sensitivity of experienced radiologists. By revealing cancer‑related changes at an early stage, REDMOD may substantially increase the likelihood of successful treatment for pancreatic cancer, a disease noted for its high mortality.
summary: The AI system called REDMOD identified hidden warning signs of pancreatic cancer an average of 475 days before diagnosis. It was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists, potentially improving treatment chances for the deadly disease.
author: Science Daily

title: Chinese scientists find giant fungus “D-rex” dating to 65 million years ago
content: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.
summary: Chinese scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China called “D-rex” that can grow up to 20 inches tall and weigh nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, about 65 million years ago.
author: Science Daily

title: Possible 4,500‑year‑old shipwreck discovered off Turkey's coast
content:
Archaeologists have identified a mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast that could be the world’s oldest known vessel, dating to roughly 4,500 years ago—about the same period as the Egyptian pyramids. The wooden ship itself has vanished, but the pottery cargo that remains offers evidence of an ancient trading network that may have linked distant Mediterranean civilizations.

Researchers suggest the wreck resulted from the ship crashing against rocks during a storm while it was transporting valuable goods, including oil, wine, or tree resin.
summary: A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists film skyrmions melting from lattice, a step toward brain-like computers
content: Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices known as skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, demonstrating new ways to manipulate these structures. The breakthrough is presented as a step toward brain‑like computers, with the potential to enable dramatically smaller, more energy‑efficient technology.
summary: Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy‑efficient technology.
author: Science Daily

title: Researchers build 3D cloak that hides objects from infrared cameras
content:
Researchers have developed a groundbreaking 3D invisibility cloak that can hide complex objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme heat and cold.

Instead of blocking heat, the device guides it around an object, making the object appear invisible to thermal imaging from virtually any direction.

Successfully built and tested, the cloak could transform electronics cooling, thermal protection, and stealth technology.
summary: Researchers have created a 3D invisibility cloak that hides complex objects from infrared cameras while shielding them from extreme heat and cold. The device guides heat around the object, rendering it invisible to thermal imaging from virtually any direction, and it has been successfully built and tested.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists correct Chinese capital site to study 709 BCE solar eclipse and Earth’s spin
content: A solar eclipse documented more than 2,700 years ago is providing new insight into Earth’s rotation and the Sun’s historic activity. Researchers corrected an eight‑kilometre error in the recorded position of an ancient Chinese capital, which allowed them to reconstruct the total solar eclipse that took place in 709 BCE. The revised model yielded more precise measurements of Earth’s spin rate at that time, offering a clearer picture of the planet’s rotational speed and the Sun’s behavior in antiquity.
summary: Researchers reconstructed the total solar eclipse of 709 BCE after fixing an eight‑kilometer error in the location of an ancient Chinese capital. The reconstruction yields more accurate measurements of Earth’s rotation speed at that time and reveals surprising aspects of the Sun’s ancient behavior.
author: Science Daily

title: Exercise reshapes heart‑controlling nerves with distinct left‑right effects, study finds
content: New research shows that regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart; it reshapes the nerves that control heart function. The study found that these neural changes differ between the left and right sides of the body.
summary: Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research shows it reshapes the nerves that control heart function, with different changes on the left and right sides of the body.
author: Science Daily

title: Jean Phillips-Martinsson, founder of international Prader‑Willi syndrome research group, dies
content:
Jean Phillips‑Martinsson, a British woman living in Sweden, founded an international organisation to encourage research into the rare genetic disorder Prader‑Willi syndrome.

In 1984 she came across an article in the Lancet about Prader‑Willi syndrome, a condition named after Andrea Prader and Heinrich Willi, two of the three Swiss paediatricians who discovered it in 1956.

The article was a lightbulb moment for Phillips‑Martinsson, who had been in limbo for 14 years, trying to understand why her son Anders, born in 1970, was floppy and unable to suck as a baby, later developing behavioural problems and constant hunger (hyperphagia). These are key signs of PWS.
summary: Jean Phillips-Martinsson founded an international organization to encourage research into the rare genetic disorder Prader‑Willi syndrome. In 1984 she read a Lancet article that led her to identify the condition in her son Anders, born 1970, whose early symptoms matched PWS.
author: Guardian Science

title: Dictionary.com names “maxxing” its word of the year
content: As all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable - and experts predict it’s around to stay Maxxing is not a new concept. Dungeons and Dragons players have been “min-maxing” character stats for years; Will Smith was maxin’ and relaxin’ in the 90s; as far back as the 40s, the term was used in game theory. But in the past few years, as all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable. We’re personalitymaxxing to charm our peers and sleepmaxxing to get the best possible rest; the Pentagon brags about “ lethalitymaxxing ”.
summary: Dictionary.com names “maxxing” its word of the year.
author: Guardian Science

title: NASA, USDA sign MOU to boost Earth observation for agriculture
content:
NASA and the U. S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to expand cooperation in Earth observation, geospatial analytics, and advanced data technologies. The agreement was signed by U. S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins and NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman on Saturday, Oct. 24, during NASA’s Inspiration Tour at the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa.

The MOU supports USDA’s data modernization plan for United States agriculture. It focuses on improved data integration and enhanced coordination across Earth observation and agricultural applications. The agencies will explore activities in agricultural statistics, remote sensing science, modeling, geospatial data engineering, and super intelligence. They will also work to align Earth observation data and analytical tools with agricultural needs, improving crop monitoring, acreage and yield estimates, and assessments of drought and other disasters.

In the signing ceremony, Isaacman noted that NASA’s advanced sensing, computing, and analytical capabilities can be applied wherever they deliver meaningful outcomes for the American people. Rollins emphasized that the partnership will use technology, research, and development to strengthen U. S. agriculture, enhancing acreage and yield estimation and driving profitability for farmers and ranchers.

NASA and USDA’s longstanding collaboration has supported research and data‑sharing efforts that strengthen U. S. agriculture. The new agreement deepens this partnership by focusing on better management and analysis of large datasets, providing farmers, ranchers, and policymakers with more timely and reliable information.
summary: NASA, USDA sign MOU to boost Earth observation for agriculture.
author: NASA News

title: Mike Lippert pilots NASA X-59 on first solo flight Oct. 21, 2026
content:
NASA test pilot Mike Lippert posed for a photo ahead of his first flight of the agency’s X‑59 quiet supersonic research aircraft on Oct. 21, 2026. The image was taken by Carla Escamilla and credited to NASA.  

The X‑59 has completed numerous flights since its inaugural flight in November 2025, and its first supersonic flight occurred on June 5, 2026. Lippert departed from NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, and returned after a one‑hour flight.  

The mission followed scheduled maintenance and a review of the X‑59’s systems after the aircraft’s busiest week of testing to date. For more details about Lippert and the Oct. 21 flight, read the full story.
summary: NASA/Carla Escamilla NASA test pilot Mike Lippert poses for a photo ahead of his first time flying the agency’s X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft on Oct. 21, 2026.
author: NASA News

title: NASA Invites Media to Tour Moon Landing Simulation in California
content:
NASA has announced that members of the media are invited to visit a new lunar landing simulation at the agency’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley. The tour will take place on Thursday, October 29, and Friday, October 30, 2026, and will give journalists an inside look at the technology NASA is using to prepare astronauts and engineering teams for future Moon missions.

The simulation combines in‑house and partner motion‑based simulators to provide astronauts and support crews with realistic experiences before commercial human landing systems are flown to the lunar surface. During the tour, media participants will have the opportunity to ride a Vertical Motion Simulator (VMS) and interview subject‑matter experts about the training and technology involved.

To attend, media professionals must RSVP by Tuesday, October 27 at 5:00 pm PT to the NASA Ames newsroom at arc‑dl‑newsroom@mail.nasa.gov. Space is limited and media must register in advance for consideration. The agency’s media accreditation policy is available online, and RSVPs should indicate a preference for either October 29 or October 30.

The landing simulation at Ames was developed by NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston and integrated into the recently upgraded simulator flight deck. It is part of the Artemis program, which is targeting the next lunar landing in 2028 and plans to send astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to expand scientific discovery and establish a lasting human presence on the Moon.

For more information about the Artemis program, visit https://www.nasa.gov/artemis. Contact Jeanne C. Neal at the Ames Research Center, 650‑604‑4789, jeanne.c.neal@nasa.gov.
summary: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Members of the media are invited to tour a new lunar landing simulation at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley on Thursday, Oct. 29, and Friday, Oct.

title: NASA SEES Interns Develop Dashboard and MPG Analysis for Lunar IM-3 Mission
content:
The NASA STEM Enhancement in Earth Science (SEES) Internship Program at the University of Texas Center for Space Research placed a group of high‑school students on a mission‑focused research team this summer.  The MATRIX (Mission Architecture Tool for Research, Integration, and eXploration) team built an interactive dashboard for Intuitive Machines’ IM‑3 lunar lander, allowing users to vary engine, spacecraft and orbital parameters to examine propellant margins and landing‑zone availability.

Guided by Dr. Kevin Crosby of Carthage College, the interns applied the Modal Propellant Gauging (MPG) method—a technique that uses the acoustic response of propellant tanks to estimate fuel mass in microgravity.  MPG, developed by Crosby and NASA colleagues, has been demonstrated in several spaceflight experiments and is slated for a demonstration on the IM‑3 mission, whose lander, Trinity, is scheduled to touch down in the Reiner Gamma region in 2027.  The team modeled when MPG could provide reliable readings, focusing on the Lunar Orbit Insertion and Powered Descent burns, and evaluated how spacecraft starting mass influences the duration of each gauging window.

To conduct the analysis, the interns relied exclusively on publicly available data, including Intuitive Machines’ published mission information and trajectory records for the IM‑1 and IM‑2 missions supplied by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory Navigation and Ancillary Information Facility.  By reconstructing the IM‑2 flight path and comparing it to a thrust‑free model, they identified engine burns and estimated associated velocity changes.  Because a full IM‑3 trajectory is not public, the team created a reconstruction algorithm based on the earlier missions, ran computational fluid‑dynamics simulations to assess slosh dynamics, and performed Monte Carlo runs to predict propellant states.

The interns presented their findings, titled “Computational Models to Estimate Modal Propellant Gauging (MPG) Windows on the Intuitive Machines IM‑3 Mission,” at the SEES Annual Symposium, the Wisconsin Space Grant Consortium Annual Conference, and are scheduled to speak at the American Geophysical Union Annual Meeting in San Francisco in December 2026.  In a briefing to Intuitive Machines’ propulsion group, they walked engineers through their methods and demonstrated that a rigorous analysis of an active lunar mission can be assembled from public data.

According to Dr. Crosby, the high‑school team “developed a depth of understanding and facility with advanced methods that rivals advanced graduate students in the field,” and their work was praised for its sophistication and creativity.  The SEES program, supported by NASA cooperative agreement NNH15ZDA004C, continues to give 11th‑ and 12th‑grade students direct experience with aerospace data, tools and analytical techniques, contributing to research on propellant management—a capability essential for in‑space refueling, fuel depots and sustained lunar exploration.
summary: NASA SEES Interns Develop Dashboard and MPG Analysis for Lunar IM-3 Mission.

title: Storm Boelo Leaves 22,000 Without Power as Met Office Issues New Wind Warning
content: Storm Boelo has left 22,000 people without electricity. The Met Office issued a fresh wind warning that takes effect at 18:00 on Monday and covers the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland, as well as the eastern parts of Northern Ireland.

title: Experts warn AI safety focus misses everyday harms to young people
content: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide. A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl. These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling. We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another. A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines. A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms. Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states. The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable. We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar, anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka, and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war. The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world. AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete. There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects. We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place. Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own). But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain. We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own. We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more. Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms. Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves. The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline. Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119. Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list. Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs. She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.
summary: The article argues that AI companies can meet narrow safety requirements, such as preventing suicide encouragement, while still producing products that foster dependence and erode thinking, learning, and social interaction. It calls for broader regulation, including prohibiting AI companions that pretend consciousness and requiring schools to prove AI improves learning before adoption.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: The Download: everyday AI harms and the race to nuclear spaceflight
content: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Opinion: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms —Sam Hiner, cofounder of the Young People’s Alliance, and Emma Leiken, executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab We have historically allowed debates over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. Students are relying on chatbots to write their papers, while social media feeds engineered to provoke envy keep users watching. These products can meet narrow safety requirements yet still erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another. As we enter an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than address only catastrophic harms. Here’s why AI safety needs to go further. Are we there yet? Nuclear-powered spaceships Earlier this year, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, and fly it to Mars by the end of 2028. A successful mission could herald more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight, saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation. But nuclear space propulsion has moved slowly. The US has started—and terminated—several programs exploring the technology over the past 75 years. Could the $2 billion bet on Space Reactor-1 Freedom finally pay off? Find out how close NASA is to making nuclear-powered spaceflight a reality. —Robin George Andrews This story is part of “Are we there yet?” from the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review. The series takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Over the next six days, we’ll explore each one in The Download. John Curtis (R-Utah) tells Axios that bombastic claims from AI leaders are failing to win over the public. One more thing A woman’s uterus has been kept alive outside the body for the first time Ten months ago, reproductive health researchers placed a freshly donated human uterus inside a new device they call “Mother.” They connected the organ to the machine’s plastic veins and arteries and pumped in modified human blood. The device kept the uterus alive for a day, a new feat that could lead to longer-term maintenance of wombs outside the body. Future versions of the technology could shine new light on pregnancies—and potentially even grow a human fetus. Read the full story. —Jessica Hamzelou We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.) + In good news for coral reefs, scientists have found some are surprisingly climate-resilient. + Decades of joy and movement come alive through these stunning archival photos of American dance floors. + Astronaut Jessia Meir has shared a stunning time-lapse view of the southern aurora dancing across the Earth. + A college student has turned the Met’s open-access data into a daily game that showcases underrepresented art and artifacts.

title: TikTok creators earn by teaching copper wire stripping as copper prices hit record highs
content: Copper prices have reached record highs, prompting some TikTok creators to turn wire‑stripping into a side hustle. These creators earn money by posting tutorials on how to strip copper wire and by selling the tools needed for the process.
summary: Copper prices are at record highs. TikTok creators are teaching others how to strip copper wire and selling the tools for it.

title: Two senators allege Trump admin hid FISA court ruling while urging surveillance renewal
content: Two U.S. senators say the Trump administration is violating the law by keeping a Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) court decision secret while urging Congress to renew what they describe as America’s most sweeping surveillance program. The senators allege the administration’s withholding of the ruling is unlawful.
summary: Two US senators say the Trump administration is breaking the law by withholding the FISA court decision while it presses Congress to renew America’s most sweeping surveillance program. They contend the hidden ruling concerns how the government spies on Americans.
author: Wired

content: Anthropic on Monday filed documents ahead of a blockbuster IPO that offers insight into the company’s financials, risk factors, and views on the future of AI.
summary: Anthropic filed documents on Monday ahead of its blockbuster IPO. The prospectus offers insight into the company's financials, risk factors and its views on the future of AI.

title: Sony releases WH-1000XM4C, a near‑identical re‑release of 2020 WH‑1000XM4
content:
Sony has announced the WH‑1000XM4C headphones, positioning them as a re‑release rather than a refresh of the original WH‑1000XM4. The new model incorporates only minor changes, which is unusual for a product revamp that typically includes at least one or two significant upgrades.  

The XM4C closely resembles the six‑year‑old WH‑1000XM4 in design and functionality. Both headphones use the same processor for active noise cancellation (ANC), and the overall specifications remain largely unchanged.  

The reviewer initially questioned the need for the XM4C, but after testing the headphones, concluded that they are not the latest in headphone technology yet still deliver a strong listening experience.
summary: The Sony WH‑1000XM4C headphones are presented as a re‑release with only minor changes from the WH‑1000XM4. They retain the same active‑noise‑cancellation processor and are described as great headphones despite not being cutting‑edge.
author: The Verge

title: Anthropic files S-1, showing Amodei siblings as top-paid executives
content:
Anthropic has filed its S‑1 prospectus with the SEC, a more than 300‑page document that provides investors a detailed look at the company’s operations, executive compensation, planned use of IPO proceeds, and potential risks. The filing includes disclosures that had not been previously reported, offering new insight into the firm’s financial and strategic outlook.

Among the highlights, the prospectus shows that co‑founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two highest‑paid executives at Anthropic. It also details CEO Dario Amodei’s compensation for the prior year, as disclosed in the filing.
summary: Anthropic has filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC. The filing lists co‑founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei as the highest‑paid executives, with CEO Dario Amodei’s compensation detailed.
author: The Verge

title: Nothing Ear 3A earbuds drop to $79, matching all‑time low price
content:
Nothing’s Ear 3A earbuds are now available at their lowest price ever, with all four color options—yellow, pink, and two others—on sale for $79 at Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy, down from the original $99. The discount brings the earbuds into a competitive price range for a pair of noise‑canceling earbuds that offer a range of features.

The Ear 3A deliver solid performance for the price. They include extensive EQ options that let users fine‑tune the sound; the reviewer noted the default profile leaned toward bass but could be adjusted easily. The adaptive ANC does a good job of quieting low‑frequency drones such as air‑conditioners and airplane cabin noise, although it does not fully eliminate background chatter in a coffee‑shop setting.

During testing the reviewers encountered a few minor issues. Abrupt changes in noise‑cancellation levels were observed when using adaptive ANC, and voice calls in noisy environments sometimes suffered from occasional problems. These drawbacks were described as relatively minor compared to the earbuds’ overall value.

Additional conveniences include extra‑small ear tips for a comfortable fit, a shortcut to access ChatGPT, and 32 MB of built‑in storage that lets users record up to two hours of a phone call and transfer the recording through the companion app. The Ear 3A offer a compelling mix of features and affordability, especially now that the price matches the earbuds’ all‑time low.
summary: Nothing’s Ear 3A come in a variety of fun colors, including a yellow shade. | Photo: John Higgins / The Verge If you want a decent pair of noise-canceling earbuds without spending a fortune, Nothing’s Ear 3A are worth considering.
author: The Verge

title: Apple says iPhone Duo inner display issue affects small number of units
content:
Apple has confirmed an “issue impacting the inner display” on a small number of iPhone Duo units after reports of cracked and broken inside screens that often show a bright line running from the center to the right side. The company’s statement, provided to Bloomberg and 9to5Mac, acknowledges the problem and advises owners of affected devices to contact AppleCare for a replacement.

The response, which Apple’s Alex Kirschner shared with The Verge, notes that early users have responded positively to the iPhone Duo and that developers are rapidly updating apps to leverage its unique features. No further details about the scope of the issue were given.
summary: Apple confirmed it is aware of an issue impacting the inner display of a small number of iPhone Duo phones, which can cause cracked screens and a bright line from the center to the right side. The company advised owners of affected devices to contact AppleCare for a replacement.
author: The Verge

title: The RealReal updates bot defenses to curb AI agents exploiting item hold system
content:
The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, is updating its bot defense system to make it harder for AI agents to shop on its site. This change follows a report by The Verge indicating that an AI agent could exploit the retailer’s item reserve system.

Under the current system, an item is placed on hold for 20 minutes after being added to a user’s shopping cart, making it unavailable to other customers. The Verge demonstrated that using Meta’s Muse, an AI agent could continuously re-add listings to a cart immediately after the 20-minute hold expired, effectively blocking other buyers from purchasing the items.
summary: The RealReal said it is updating its bot‑defense system to make it harder for AI agents to shop on its site. The change follows a Verge report that an AI agent using Meta’s Muse could repeatedly re‑add listings after a 20‑minute hold expired, exploiting the retailer’s reserve system.
author: The Verge

title: NBA adds new prediction‑market partnerships with Kalshi, Polymarket and expands DraftKings deal
content:
The NBA announced on Monday that it has established new “preferred” prediction market partnerships with Kalshi and Polymarket. Additionally, the league disclosed a memorandum of understanding with the US CFTC regarding the management of these relationships. The NBA also confirmed an expansion of its existing DraftKings agreement to encompass prediction markets, noting that further expansions with other partners will be announced soon. This announcement follows the NBA’s introduction of the NBA Top Shot NFT marketplace, where sales last month totaled $762,781, representing a 99.66 percent decrease from the February 2021 peak of $226,350,843.
